How are gluons easier to detect than neutrinos despite interacting with even fewer particles?

Gluons are charged particles that make up the particles that make up an atom (protons and neutrons). The force between gluons increases the further away they are from each other, which is the exact opposite of the forces that make up atoms.

Neutrinos are electrically neutral and very rarely interact with other particles. They also don't make up particles themselves, but are created during fusion and other radioactive events. Neutrinos also are able to change form after they were created:

Neutrinos are now understood to oscillate between different flavors in flight. That is, an electron neutrino produced in a beta decay reaction may arrive in a detector as a muon or tau neutrino. This oscillation requires that the different neutrino flavors have different masses, although these masses have been shown to be tiny.

Gluons aren't particles of matter, they are force carriers like a photon. We detect them via the effect they have on matter.

Neutrinos are matter, but their neutral charge and various other properties make them harder to detect than most matter.

Gluons are essentially the same thing as a photon (they are both force carriers) except gluons are exchanged between quarks and represent the strong force (whereas photons carry the electromagnetic force. Quarks are what make up protons and neutrons. When we smash streams of protons together in accelerator, the quarks inside the protons are torn apart; however, the strong force causes particle/anti-particle pairs to be created between the quarks. This creates a jet of quarks and gluons. These jets are easy to observe (well at least relatively easy) and occur in nearly every particle accelerator.
